title: Infra Playbook: GPU Fleet Capacity, Cloud Accounts & Networking, IaC Modules, CI/CD (2026 Best Practices)
author: Priya Kapoor
body:
Summary:
This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference's best practices for GPU fleet capacity planning, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC module design, and CI/CD for infra changes. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners who operate the GPU serving fleet and the associated cloud networking and IaC pipelines.

Goals:
- Maintain predictable capacity and cost while meeting production SLOs.
- Keep IaC modular, testable, and secure with gated CI/CD.
- Ensure network boundaries and cloud accounts follow least-privilege and auditability.
- Provide clear runbooks for common operational events (surge, OOM, failed deploys, network outage).

Scope:
- GPU fleet sizing, node types, and cushion targets.
- Cloud accounts structure (org, landing zones, shared services).
- VPC design, peering/transit, and egress controls for inference clusters.
- Terraform module patterns, versioning, and registry conventions.
- CI/CD pipelines for plan/validate/apply, policy checks, and canary rollouts.
- Runbooks for capacity incidents, deployments, and upgrades.

Ownership:
- Fleet capacity and autoscaling: infra-capacity team (pager: #infra-capacity).
- Terraform modules and registries: infra-iac team.
- CI/CD pipelines and gating: infra-ci team.
- Network architecture and cloud accounts: cloud-platform team.

Key SLOs and operational thresholds (production inference clusters):
| Metric | Target | Alerting threshold | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 99th percentile serving latency (token gen) | < 120 ms | > 150 ms for 5m | Measured at edge/backplane for p95/p99 per model route |
| GPU utilization (avg per-node, 1h) | 55-75% | > 85% sustained 15m | Target favors headroom for traffic spikes |
| Node CPU usage (avg) | < 70% | > 90% 10m | Signals background processes/OOM risk |
| Queue length (requests waiting for batch) | < 50 ms average | > 200 ms 5m | Long queues indicate undersized fleet or batching misconfig |
| Reserved capacity cushion | 20% of baseline | < 15% -> capacity scale-up | Cushion for burst traffic and AZ failures |

Capacity planning and sizing guidelines:
1. Baseline measurement:
   - Collect 14-day rolling average QPS and token/sec by model and route.
   - Capture peak-2 (second-highest daily peak) to avoid overfitting to outliers.
2. Estimate GPU units required:
   - Measure model throughput per GPU for representative batch sizes and seq lengths.
   - Required GPUs = ceil((peak_tokens_per_sec / tokens_per_sec_per_gpu) * (1 + cushion)).
   - Example: peak_tokens=120k/s, gpu_throughput=4k tokens/s -> baseline 30 GPUs + 20% cushion = 36 GPUs.
3. Factor in heterogenous node types (A100, H100, L2-accelerated):
   - Prefer homogeneous pools per model family to simplify placement.
   - Use autoscaling groups per node-type with consistent labels/tags.
4. Autoscaling policy recommendations:
   - Scale on tokens/sec and GPU utilization combined.
   - Minimum nodes = baseline for reserved capacity; max nodes = baseline * 4 (soft).
   - Cooldown: 3m for scale-up, 10m for scale-down.

Cloud accounts & networking patterns:
- Organization structure:
  - org-root/
  - \u251c\u2500 security (shared infra: logs, guardrails)
  - \u251c\u2500 shared-services (bastions, monitoring, artifact registries)
  - \u251c\u2500 prod (inference clusters, stateful infra)
  - \u2514\u2500 staging/dev (mirror of prod with reduced capacity)
- VPC & subnet layout:
  - One VPC per environment (prod/staging/dev) per region.
  - Subnets: public (ingress LB), private (inference nodes), db/management (restricted).
  - AZ-aware placement: maintain at least 2 AZs for prod clusters.
- Network security:
  - Use centralized transit (TGW) or cloud-native transit gateway to connect shared-services and prod VPCs.
  - Egress control: route through NAT + egress proxies; all outbound to third parties must go via approved proxy.
  - Firewall rules: deny-by-default, allow lists for model registry, metrics ingest, key management endpoints.
- Service endpoints and peering:
  - Allow direct VPC endpoints for S3/object stores, ECR/Azure Container Registry, and KMS to avoid public egress.

Terraform / IaC module conventions:
- Module registry structure (internal):
  - modules/networking/{vpc,subnet,tgw,security-groups}
  - modules/gpu-cluster/{node-pool,k8s-nodegroup,gpu-device-plugin}
  - modules/observability/{prometheus,logging,datadog-integrations}
  - modules/iam/{roles,service-accounts}
- Module design principles:
  - Single responsibility: each module manages one resource abstraction.
  - Inputs/outputs typed and documented. Keep outputs minimal (ARNs/IDs only).
  - Defaults safe-for-prod (e.g., encrypted storage, private endpoints enabled).
  - Version pin modules in root terragrunt/terragrunt.hcl or Terraform root module. Do not use unpinned module refs in prod.
- Example Terraform snippet (for node pool):
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.4"
}
module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@internal/modules.git//gpu-cluster/node-pool?ref=v1.3.0"
  name   = "inference-a100-pool"
  instance_type = "nvidia-a100-80gb"
  desired_count = 12
  spot_enabled  = true
  tags = {
    team = "infra-capacity"
    stack = "inference"
  }
}
- State and secrets:
  - Use remote state in the centralized state backend with per-environment state files (S3 + DynamoDB or cloud equivalent).
  - Secrets should not be in Terraform state; use external secret manager (Vault/KMS) and reference via data sources at runtime.

CI/CD and pipeline guidelines:
1. Pipeline stages (recommended):
   - lint (tfsec, tflint), fmt check, module-version pin validation
   - terraform plan (env-isolation) with auto-comment on PR (Atlantis/GitHub Actions)
   - policy checks (OPA/Conftest) and security scanning (snyk/tern for images)
   - integration test (apply to ephemeral environment or use plan-only approval harness)
   - approval gates for prod apply (manual trigger + 2 approvers for infra changes > threshold)
   - terraform apply (automated for non-prod via Atlantis; manual for prod with scheduled windows)
2. Rollout strategy for infra changes impacting serving nodes:
   - Canary apply to a single AZ and 10% of nodes. Validate metrics (latency, error-rate) for 30m.
   - Gradual roll-forward: 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% with health checks between steps.
   - Automatic rollback if p99 latency regresses by > 20% or error rate increases > 1% absolute.
3. Pull request expectations:
   - Every Terraform change requires a changelog entry in PR body, owner tag, and associated runbook if it touches critical infra.
   - All module bumps must include a compatibility note and a migration plan where necessary.

Policy & compliance checks:
- Mandatory checks on prod branches: iam-privilege-check, s3-public-check, kms-encryption-check.
- Use OPA/Rego policies stored in central repo. CI should reject PRs that fail policy unless bypass with documented exception and approver.

Monitoring and observability configuration:
- Metrics to expose from node pools: gpu_utilization, gpu_memory_used, queue_length, inference_latency_p50/p95/p99, node_drain_events.
- Dashboards: per-cluster, per-model-route breakdown, cost-per-token trend.
- Alerts (examples):
  - gpu_mem_pressure: any node > 90% GPU memory for 5m -> Sev2 (pager).
  - unexpected_scale_down: sudden removal of >20% nodes in 10m -> Sev1.
  - plan-apply-drift: if terraform-drift detection flags a difference for 30m -> oncall.

Runbooks (quick action steps):
- Incident: GPU OOM / Memory Pressure\n  1. Pager fires to #infra-capacity and oncall. Check cluster GPU memory metrics and pod logs.
  2. Identify model(s) with increased memory usage: kubectl top pods -n inference | grep -i gpu
  3. If a single model causing OOM, patch model route to fallback lightweight variant and restart pods in affected nodepool: kubectl rollout restart deploy/<model-deploy> -n inference
  4. If node-level OOM, cordon node and drain: kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
  5. Scale up node pool if sustained memory pressure persists: terraform apply -var 'desired_count=+' or use autoscaler.
  6. Post-incident: run replay test with load to validate stability and file postmortem.

- Incident: Capacity surge / sustained high utilization\n  1. Verify traffic spike source (ingress logs, api-gateway).
  2. If legitimate business spike, trigger emergency scale-up (increase desired_count by 30%) and notify product owner.
  3. If spike looks anomalous, enable rate-limiting or fallback to lower-cost model variant via routing policy.
  4. Update capacity forecast and consider increasing cushion for that model route.

- Deployment rollback (failed canary):\n  1. Abort rollout and revert Terraform module change (git revert or rollback to prior module ref).
  2. Apply revert to canary AZ first, validate, then apply to remaining AZs.
  3. Run smoke tests and monitor p99 for 60m before marking incident resolved.

Onboarding checklist (new infra engineer):
- Access: cloud console, org admin read-only, GitHub, CI, Slack channels (#infra-ops, #infra-capacity).
- Read this playbook + infra-iac-team-wiki.
- Run local Terraform plan for staging and deploy a small ephemeral cluster to learn all steps.
- Pair with infra-iac engineer for first prod PR.

Appendix: quick command cheatsheet:
- Check GPU utilization (k8s node exporter / nvidia-smi): kubectl top nodes --selector=pool=inference && kubectl get pods -o wide -n inference
- Cordoning & draining node: kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
- Terraform plan (prod): TERRAFORM_BACKEND=prod terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars
- Applying module bump (staged): git checkout -b module-bump && update module ref && gh pr create --title "module: bump network v1.4.0" && wait for CI checks

Next review cycle:
- This playbook should be reviewed quarterly or after any major incident that impacts capacity or networking.
- Owners: infra-capacity (quarterly), cloud-platform (network sections), infra-iac (IaC modules), infra-ci (CI/CD pipeline sections).
